hirag.pageDescription: A transparent explanation of our hierarchical retrieval architecture, based on cutting-edge research with domain-specific adaptations for ancient philosophy scholarship.

overview.title: Overview & Paper Citation
overview.basedOn: Our implementation is based on the HiRAG (Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation) architecture described in:
overview.innovationDescription: HiRAG extends standard GraphRAG by introducing a three-level hierarchical knowledge structure:
overview.localKnowledge: Local Knowledge: Specific entities retrieved via semantic search
overview.globalKnowledge: Global Knowledge: Community-level summaries providing thematic context
overview.bridgeKnowledge: Bridge Knowledge: Shortest paths between entities across communities
overview.paperResults: Paper results show HiRAG achieves 54-64% win rate vs. GraphRAG and 52-66% vs. LightRAG across benchmark datasets.

implemented.title: What We Implemented from the Paper

hierarchical.title: 1. Hierarchical Structure
hierarchical.level0: 14 global summaries covering major philosophical themes (determinism, moral responsibility, divine providence)
hierarchical.level1: 11 community summaries organized by philosophical schools (Stoic, Epicurean, Peripatetic, Patristic)
hierarchical.level2: 503 individual entity nodes (philosophers, concepts, arguments, works)

bridge.title: 2. Shortest-Path Bridge Detection
bridge.algorithm: Algorithm 2 from paper: For each retrieved community, we select top-m key entities (m=2), then compute shortest paths between entities from different communities.
bridge.impact: Impact: Provides 38-83% recall coverage of both local and global knowledge, creating semantic chains that bridge philosophical schools.

perCommunity.title: 3. Per-Community Key Entity Selection
perCommunity.description: Instead of selecting top-k entities overall, we select top-m entities per community (m=2 as recommended in paper). This ensures diverse coverage across philosophical schools rather than over-representation of dominant communities.

threeLevel.title: 4. Three-Level Retrieval
threeLevel.description: Each query retrieves knowledge at all three levels simultaneously, then blends them for comprehensive context that spans from specific textual details to broad historical patterns.

adaptations.title: Our Adaptations & Improvements
adaptations.summariesIntro: While the paper generates summaries dynamically using DeepSeek-V3, we use pre-computed summaries created with:
adaptations.humanReviewDesc: All summaries validated by domain expert (Romain Girardi)

quality.title: Superior Quality
quality.description: Opus & GPT-5 > DeepSeek-V3 in reasoning depth and scholarly accuracy

consistency.title: Consistency
consistency.description: Same high-quality summaries for every query vs. variable dynamic generation

performance.title: Performance
performance.description: No generation overhead; summaries loaded instantly from pre-computed store

rigor.title: Scholarly Rigor
rigor.description: Human-reviewed summaries ensure accuracy for academic research

gmm.title: ❌ GMM Clustering
gmm.description: Paper's Gaussian Mixture Models → We use Leiden algorithm (better for graph-structured data)

sparsity.title: ❌ Cluster Sparsity Stopping
sparsity.description: Paper's iterative convergence → We have fixed 3-level pre-computed hierarchy (more practical)

metaAttributes.title: ❌ Meta-Attributes
metaAttributes.description: Paper's explicit meta-summaries → Already implicit in our node type system (person, concept, argument, work)

adaptations.netResultDescription: We implement the core algorithmic innovations from the paper (shortest-path bridges, per-community selection, hierarchical retrieval) while improving on the summary quality baseline through pre-computed expert-validated content. This gives us the paper's structural benefits with higher-quality knowledge representation.

technical.title: Technical Implementation
technical.backendServiceDesc: Implements HiRAGService with hierarchical indexing, shortest-path bridge detection, and three-level retrieval
technical.summaryLoaderDesc: Loads pre-computed Opus/GPT-5 summaries from hierarchical_communities_opus.json
technical.reproducibilityDesc: All implementation details, including summary generation prompts and bridge detection algorithms, are available in our open-source repository. The pre-computed summaries (generated October 27, 2025) are versioned and can be regenerated with the same process.
technical.reproducibilityMetadata: Summary metadata includes: model used (gpt-5-high), authors (GPT 5-high & Romain Girardi), final reviewer (Romain Girardi), and generation timestamp for full transparency.

comparison.title: Quality Comparison & Expected Performance
comparison.performanceIntro: Based on the paper's ablation study (Table 3), our implementation should achieve:
comparison.winRate: 54-64% win rate vs. standard GraphRAG (full HiRAG benefits)
comparison.recallCoverage: 38-83% recall coverage from bridge knowledge (paper's Table 2)
comparison.higherQuality: Potentially higher than paper due to superior summary quality (Opus > DeepSeek)
comparison.consistency: More consistent answers due to pre-computed vs. dynamic generation
comparison.academicNoteText: This implementation faithfully reproduces the core algorithmic contributions of Huang et al.'s HiRAG architecture while adapting the summary generation component for production quality and scholarly rigor. All adaptations are clearly documented here and in our codebase. We acknowledge the original paper's innovations and recommend citing both the original work and our implementation when referencing this system.

summary.title: Summary
summary.tookFromPaper: What we took from the paper
summary.tookFromPaperText: Hierarchical knowledge structure, shortest-path bridge detection (Algorithm 2), per-community key entity selection, and three-level retrieval architecture.
summary.adaptedText: Pre-computed expert-validated summaries (Opus + GPT-5 + human review) instead of dynamic DeepSeek generation, ensuring higher quality and consistency.
summary.whyText: This gives us the paper's structural innovations with superior knowledge representation, combining cutting-edge retrieval algorithms with domain-expert scholarly rigor.

about.title: About
about.projectIntro: (Ἐλευθερία = freedom + IA = Intelligence Artificielle) emerged from the need for a comprehensive, structured database documenting ancient philosophical debates on free will, fate, and moral responsibility. This research infrastructure was developed as part of doctoral research at Université Côte d'Azur, investigating how early Christian authors conceptualized human freedom and agency.
about.projectContext: When examining the notion of free will among the first Christian authors, it became clear that existing resources lacked the systematic structure necessary for computational analysis and cross-referential research. The philosophical landscape spanning from Classical Greek thought (4th c. BCE) through Late Antiquity (6th c. CE) is incredibly rich, with complex networks of influence, argumentation, and conceptual evolution that traditional bibliographic approaches struggle to capture.
about.projectDetails: This database represents an independent effort to address that gap. Every node, edge, and citation has been meticulously researched and verified against ancient sources and modern scholarship. The project integrates 2,193 philosophical entities (persons, works, concepts, arguments) connected through 8,616 relationships, alongside 189 ancient works (16,968 passages) with full lemmatization support.
about.projectGoal: The goal is to provide researchers, students, and anyone interested in ancient philosophy with a FAIR-compliant (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) resource that combines traditional philological rigor with modern computational capabilities. The integration of GraphRAG (Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation) enables semantic search and question-answering while maintaining complete provenance and citation tracking.
about.projectNote: Note: This database represents a personal research initiative. All aspects—from conceptualization and philological work to data curation, technical implementation, and interface design—were undertaken individually to support doctoral research needs.
about.authorTitle2: PhD Candidate in Ancient Languages and Literature / Theology
about.authorBio: Romain Girardi is a doctoral candidate in a joint PhD program (cotutelle internationale) between **Université Côte d'Azur** and **Université de Genève** (since January 2024), working under the supervision of Prof. Arnaud Zucker (CEPAM, UMR 7264) and Prof. Andreas Dettwiler (Faculté autonome de théologie protestante). His dissertation examines the emergence and conceptualization of free will among early Christian authors, exploring why references to human freedom proliferate in 2nd-century CE Christian literature despite being absent from biblical texts and relatively rare in earlier philosophical works.
about.interest1: Ancient philosophy of action and moral responsibility
about.interest2: Stoic and Peripatetic theories of determinism and freedom
about.interest5: Conceptual history and terminology evolution (Greek to Latin)
about.interest6: Digital humanities and knowledge graph approaches to ancient texts
about.degree1: Joint PhD in Ancient Languages and Literature (UniCA) / Theology (UNIGE) (2024–present)
about.degree3: Master's degree in Classical Letters, distinction (2019)
about.degree4: Bachelor's degree in Classical Letters, distinction (2017)
about.hiragDesc: This database implements HiRAG (Hierarchical Retrieval-Augmented Generation), extending GraphRAG by organizing knowledge across abstraction levels. Instead of treating all nodes equally, HiRAG respects the natural hierarchy: authors write works, works discuss concepts, concepts appear in debates. This multi-level reasoning produces more nuanced scholarly answers with proper attribution.
about.philoDesc: All Greek and Latin texts undergo manual verification. Lemmatization uses LAULA (Latin) and PAULA (Greek) morphological analyzers to enable lemma-based search. Every knowledge graph node is grounded in primary sources (ancient texts) or secondary literature (modern scholarship) with full bibliographic provenance.
about.techStack: React 19 + TypeScript + Vite + Tailwind CSS frontend, FastAPI + Python backend, PostgreSQL (structured data) + Qdrant (vector embeddings), Cytoscape.js for network visualization, GraphRAG pipeline with Gemini API, Cloudflare Workers (production deployment)

embedding.definition: A list of numbers (3,072) that represents the meaning of text. Similar meanings have similar vectors.

vector.definition: A list of numbers. In EleutherIA, each text is represented by 3,072 numbers.

semanticSearch.definition: Finding texts by meaning, not just keywords. "Free will" also finds "liberty" and "ἐφ' ἡμῖν".

knowledgeGraph.definition: A network of interconnected concepts. Nodes = entities, Edges = relationships.

graphrag.definition: Graph-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation. Combines KG + search + AI for Q&A.

lemma.definition: The dictionary form of a word. "λόγου" → "λόγος". Enables finding all word forms.

rrf.definition: Reciprocal Rank Fusion. A formula for combining multiple ranked lists into one.

ctsUrn.definition: Canonical Text Services Uniform Resource Name. Standard citation format for ancient texts.

fairPrinciples.definition: Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable. International principles for open data.

llm.definition: Large Language Model. The AI that synthesizes answers from context.

cosineSimilarity.definition: Measure of vector similarity. 1.0 = identical, 0.0 = completely different.

qdrant.definition: Vector database optimized for storing and searching embeddings efficiently.
